Superconductivity in the two-dimensional Hubbard model
revealed by neural quantum states

Christopher Roth Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA    Ao Chen Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Center for Electronic Correlations and Magnetism, University of Augsburg, 86135 Augsburg, Germany    Anirvan Sengupta Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA Affiliation: Center for Computational Mathematics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, New York 10010, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, Rutgers University, Piscataway, New Jersey 08854, USA    Antoine Georges Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA Affiliation: Collège de France, 11 place Marcelin Berthelot, 75005 Paris, France Affiliation: CPHT, CNRS, École Polytechnique, IP Paris, F-91128 Palaiseau, France Affiliation: DQMP, Université de Genève, 24 quai Ernest Ansermet, CH-1211 Genève, Suisse
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Whether the ground state of the square lattice Hubbard model exhibits superconductivity remains a major open question, central to understanding high temperature cuprate superconductors and ultra-cold fermions in optical lattices. Numerical studies have found evidence for stripe-ordered states and superconductivity at strong coupling but the phase diagram remains controversial. Here, we show that one can resolve the subtle energetics of metallic, superconducting, and stripe phases using a new class of neural quantum state (NQS) wavefunctions that extend hidden fermion determinant states to Pfaffians. We simulate several hundred electrons using fast Pfaffian algorithms allowing us to measure off-diagonal long range order. At strong coupling and low hole-doping, we find that a non-superconducting filled stripe phase prevails, while superconductivity coexisting with partially-filled stripes is stabilized by a negative next neighbor hopping t′t^{\prime}, with |t′|>0.1|t^{\prime}|>0.1. At larger doping levels, we introduce momentum-space correlation functions to mitigate finite size effects that arise from weakly-bound pairs. These provide evidence for uniform d-wave superconductivity at U=4U=4, even when t′=0t^{\prime}=0. Our results highlight the potential of NQS approaches, and provide a fresh perspective on superconductivity in the square lattice Hubbard model.

I Introduction

It was suggested early on [2, 28, 30, 39] that antiferromagnetic superexchange in the presence of strong repulsive interactions may be responsible for the high-temperature superconductivity (SC) observed in copper oxide compounds (cuprates). In this context, the two-dimensional square lattice Hubbard model provides the simplest framework in which this mechanism can be put to the test [35, 3].

Establishing the ground-state phase diagram of this model has proven very challenging because of the presence of phenomenologically distinct states with extremely close energies. In recent years, computational methods have nonetheless made great strides on this problem, so that some properties are now established without a shred of doubt. For example, all computational methods agree that at strong coupling and 1/81/8-doping, the ground-state of the Hubbard model with only nearest-neighbor hopping hosts a charge and spin-density wave - with doped holes forming insulating stripes [49, 45, 34, 44, 19, 33]. All methods also agree that the model displays a strong response to an applied d-wave pairing field in a range of doping levels [24, 19, 34]. More broadly, there is now a fairly good agreement on the possible competing or intertwined long-range orders.

We are now at an exciting frontier where the goal is to assess which of these possible phases truly has the lowest energy, and computational methods are becoming accurate enough to address this challenge. An outstanding question, for example, is whether the insulating stripe ground-state can give way to a d-wave superconductor when a next nearest-neighbor hopping t′t^{\prime} is turned on. A remarkable recent work  [44] combining constrained-path auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo (CP-AFQMC) and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) simulations with careful consideration of boundary conditions recently answered this question affirmatively, yet this still remains a source of debate  [23, 21, 48, 22, 12, 29].

Another thread of research is understanding the pure Hubbard model, with t′=0t^{\prime}=0, for which cold fermionic gases in optical lattices provide an analog quantum simulation platform. These experiments have recently reached unprecedentedly low temperatures where collective effects are expected to emerge[46, 7, 25]. While it is known that this model has a superconducting phase with an exponentially small order parameter in the U≪tU\ll t limit [36, 27, 15] it is important to establish whether pairing becomes significantly larger when on-site repulsion is increased. Answering this question, which is still an ongoing source of debate [34, 14, 41], may help to inform future choices for experiments.

We examine both of these regimes, the t−t′t-t^{\prime} model at strong coupling, and the pure Hubbard model in a range of coupling favorable for d-wave superconductivity. Our simulations use the recently introduced hidden fermion Pfaffian states (HFPS) [11]. Pfaffian wavefunctions provide an expressive ansatz which can be naturally combined with deep neural networks in order to capture charge, spin and superconducting orders and their interplay. Our work, in conjunction with reference [18], extends fermionic neural quantum states (fNQS) simulations to much larger systems of several hundred electrons.

First, we simulate the t−t′t-t^{\prime} model at U/t=8U/t=8 and 1/81/8-doping. In agreement with other numerical methods, we find an insulating stripe phase at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 [45, 50], which transitions to a shorter period (”partially-filled” 11 1 The filling of a stripe refers to the ratio between the number of holes per domain wall and the number of sites per domain wall) stripe when a large enough negative next neighbor hopping is turned on [44, 18, 20]. Notably, we find that this partially-filled stripe exhibits superconductivity with a pairing order parameter of O⁡(10−2)O(10^{-2}), in sharp agreement with the recent handshake between DMRG and CP-AFQMC [44]. In contrast with the handshake study, which measures the linear response to an applied pairing field, we look for superconductivity by measuring the long-range behavior of pair correlation functions. Therefore, this indicates an exciting convergence between studies which differ in both their computational schemes and methods of detecting pairing.

Next, we investigate whether superconductivity with a sizable order parameter can exist without t′t^{\prime}. Here we focus on intermediate coupling U/t=4U/t=4 at 1/61/6-doping where most methods agree that stripe ordering does not take place [45, 41]. We present evidence that the ground state has fairly strong d-wave superconductivity for these parameters, which may be detectable in cold atom experiments. By running accurate simulations on large, symmetric geometries, we show that unlike the t′≠0t^{\prime}\neq 0 case, this superconductor hosts pairs with a very long coherence length. This leads to stronger finite-size effects than in the strong coupling regime, which motivates us to introduce momentum-space correlation functions that are better suited to the investigation of regimes with weakly bound pairs. This observation resolves many of the disagreements among different computational studies, as the local d-wave order parameter only captures a small fraction of the total pairing for weakly-bound pairs. Therefore, although we find robust superconductivity, it is not incompatible with the previous finding that the local d-wave order parameter is quite small [34].

Using a flexible Pfaffian-based ansatz and low-rank update algorithms, we accurately simulate the square lattice Hubbard model on large symmetric geometries, carefully accounting for finite size effects. We provide new insight into the intertwined orders and the nature of pairing, heightening our understanding of how high-TcT_{c} superconductivity may emerge from microscopic interactions.

II Methods

II.1 Hubbard model

We simulate the square lattice Hubbard model with an additional next-neighbor interaction,

H^Hub=U​∑𝐱c^𝐱,↑†​c^𝐱,↑​c^𝐱,↓†​c^𝐱,↓−∑𝐱,𝐱′∑σt𝐱𝐱′​c^𝐱,σ†​c^𝐱′,σ{\hat{H}}_{\mathrm{Hub}}=U\sum_{\bf x}{\hat{c}}^{\dagger}_{{\bf x},\uparrow}{\hat{c}}_{{\bf x},\uparrow}{\hat{c}}^{\dagger}_{{\bf x},\downarrow}{\hat{c}}_{{\bf x},\downarrow}-\sum_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}\sum_{\sigma}t_{{\bf x}{\bf x^{\prime}}}{\hat{c}}^{\dagger}_{{\bf x},\sigma}{\hat{c}}_{{\bf x^{\prime}},\sigma} (1)

Here UU represents an energy penalty from Coulomb repulsion when two electrons share a site, and the hopping amplitudes t𝐱,𝐱′t_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}} are associated with the kinetic energy gain, with t𝐱,𝐱′=tt_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}=t for nearest-neighbor hopping and t𝐱,𝐱′=t′t_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}=t^{\prime} for next nearest-neighbor hopping. Without loss of generality, we set t=1t=1.

II.2 Hidden Fermion Pfaffian States

We use the recently introduced hidden fermion Pfaffian states (HFPS) [11] as a variational wavefunction in order to simulate different regimes of the Hubbard model to high accuracy. This method extends the hidden fermion method [31] to wavefunctions with pairing.

The HFPS ansatz can be written in the following form,

ψ⁡(𝐧)=J⁡(𝐧)​Pf​(𝐧⋆(F+H⁡(𝐧)​A​HT​(𝐧))⋆𝐧),\psi({\bf n})=J({\bf n})\,\textrm{Pf}\Bigg({\bf n}\star\Big(F+H({\bf n})AH^{T}({\bf n})\Big)\star{\bf n}\Bigg), (2)

where J⁡(𝐧)J({\bf n}) is a neural network Jastrow, F is the mean field orbital matrix, and H⁡(𝐧)​A​HT​(𝐧)H({\bf n})AH^{T}({\bf n}) can be viewed as a backflow correction. The matrix AA, which is an antisymmetric matrix that describes the coupling between hidden fermions, H⁡(𝐧)H({\bf n}), has shape 2​n~×2​n~2{\tilde{n}}\times 2{\tilde{n}}, where n~{\tilde{n}} is the number of hidden fermions. If the number of hidden fermions is much smaller than the number of electrons, n~<<n{\tilde{n}}<<n, a low rank update scheme can be used to compute the ratio between the wavefunction amplitudes of Fock states that differ by a small number of electron hops. This massively speeds up Monte Carlo and allows us to access large system sizes. Both J⁡(𝐧)J({\bf n}) and H⁡(𝐧)H({\bf n}) are parametrized by a single group-convolutional neural network [13, 38]. The first n~{\tilde{n}} feature vectors are used to compute H⁡(𝐧)H({\bf n}), while the remaining are symmetry averaged to compute J⁡(𝐧)J({\bf n}). Finally, the operation ⋆\star selects the orbitals that are occupied by fermions in the Fock state (often referred to as ‘slicing’) [31, 11].

We can control the symmetry breaking unit cell of our wavefunction by choosing an appropriate block-circulant structure for FF. This allows us to target particular density wave configurations, such as filled and half-filled stripes.

In order to improve the final variational accuracy, ψ⁡(𝐧)\psi({\bf n}) is symmetry projected, so that the wavefunction has the full symmetry of the Hamiltonian,

⟨𝐧|ψ⟩=∑g∈Gψ⁡(g​𝐧).\langle{\bf n}|\psi\rangle=\sum_{g\in G}\psi({g{\bf n}}). (3)

Here, GG represents the group of symmetry operations that are broken by the unit cell. See the reference [31] for details about the hidden fermion formalism and [11] about how it is generalized to Pfaffians.

II.3 Expressivity of the Pfaffian

It has been well established that the Hubbard model has many competing phases of matter that are extremely close in energy [45]. These phases include magnetically ordered insulators, metals and potentially superconductors. There is also emerging evidence that more exotic phases, which can have both long ranged density wave and pairing order, can emerge in the presence of a next neighbor hopping t′t^{\prime} [44]. We emphasize that the Pfaffian,

⟨𝐧|ψp​f⟩=Pf​(𝐧⋆F⋆𝐧),\langle{\bf n}|\psi_{pf}\rangle=\textrm{Pf}\Big({\bf n}\star F\star{\bf n}\Big), (4)

can represent all of these phases at the mean field level.

The Pfaffian is a solution to the Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian which can be written in the following form,

H=12​∑𝐱,𝐱′Ψ𝐱†​(h𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′Δ𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′−(Δ𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′)∗−(h𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′)T)​Ψ𝐱′H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}\Psi_{\bf x}^{\dagger}\begin{pmatrix}h^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}&\Delta^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}\\ -(\Delta^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}})^{*}&-(h_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}}^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}})^{T}\end{pmatrix}\Psi_{\bf x^{\prime}}

where h𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′h^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}} and Δ𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′\Delta^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}_{{\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}} are 2×22\times 2 matrices which describe hopping and pairing respectively between up and down spins, and Ψ𝐱=(c𝐱↑,c𝐱↓,c𝐱↑†,c𝐱↓†)\Psi_{\bf x}=(c_{\bf x\uparrow},c_{\bf x\downarrow},c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\uparrow},c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\downarrow}) is a Nambu spinor. The general solution can have spin and density correlations ⟨c𝐱,σ†​c𝐱,σ′⟩≠0\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bf x,\sigma}c_{\bf x,\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle\neq 0, as well as singlet ⟨c𝐱,↑​c𝐱′,↓⟩≠0\langle c_{\bf x,\uparrow}c_{\bf x^{\prime},\downarrow}\rangle\neq 0 and triplet ⟨c𝐱,↑​c𝐱′,↑⟩≠0\langle c_{\bf x,\uparrow}c_{\bf x^{\prime},\uparrow}\rangle\neq 0 pairing.

Therefore, the Pfaffian can represent phases with intertwined charge, spin, superconducting orders, making it an ideal starting point for flexibly capturing the phases of the square lattice Hubbard model.

The Slater determinant represents a subclass of solutions to the BdG Hamiltonian where Δ𝐱,𝐱′σ,σ′=0\Delta_{\bf x,\bf x^{\prime}}^{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}=0. While it cannot represent superconducting order directly, in some cases unitary particle-hole transformations can be used to achieve this goal. However, our contention is that Pfaffian provides a more natural and expressive framework.

II.4 Optimization strategy

It is well established that NQS wavefunctions have different local minima of the variational energy, corresponding to different phases of a given Hamiltonian [4, 40]. In order to ensure that we find the phase that is a global minimum, we run several controlled optimizations starting from distinct mean field solutions. We run each trajectory by initializing FF with a plausible ground-state order, and setting J⁡(𝐧)=1J({\bf n})=1, A=0A=0 so that our initial wavefunction is the mean-field Pfaffian in Eqn. 2. The mean field orbitals, FF, are trained with exact gradient on the following Hamiltonian,

ℋ^0=ℋ^Hub(U0)+Δ0∑𝜹sign(𝜹)(c𝐱+𝜹↑†c𝐱↓†+h.c.),\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{0}=\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{Hub}}(U_{0})+\Delta_{0}\sum_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}\textrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\delta}})(c^{\dagger}_{{\bf x}+\boldsymbol{\delta}\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\downarrow}+h.c.), (5)

where 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} runs over the four nearest neighbor displacements and sign​(𝜹)\textrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{\delta}) is +1+1 for vertical bonds and −1-1 for horizontal bonds. The d-wave pinning field is necessary to initialize the wavefunction with pairing, as the best mean-field solution to ℋHub\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{Hub}} always has ⟨c𝐱,σ​c𝐱​σ′⟩=0\langle c_{\bf x,\sigma}c_{\bf x\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle=0. This is because the pairing correlations only enter quadratically through the onsite repulsion; therefore they are zero for U0>0U_{0}>0 at the mean-field level.

We can find stripes of different periodicity by constraining FF to have particular block-circulant forms, while U0U_{0} and Δ0\Delta_{0} can be used to control the strength of the magnetism and superconductivity. We have experimented with initial conditions in both regimes and find that there are distinct local minima which are close in energy but have different long range order. However, once the optimization converges to a particular ordering, the final solution is fairly insensitive to the details of the initialization, as documented below.

II.5 Detecting long-range order from correlation functions

Our simulations are performed on finite size lattices – clusters of NN sites with periodic boundary conditions – where spin, charge and lattice symmetries are preserved. Therefore, we must detect spontaneously broken symmetries by looking for long range order in two-body correlations. In this study we focus on spin,

Cs​(𝐱)=1N​∑𝐱′[⟨S^𝐱+𝐱′z​S^𝐱′z⟩−⟨S^𝐱+𝐱′z⟩​⟨S^𝐱′z⟩],C_{s}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf x^{\prime}}\Big[\braket{\hat{S}^{z}_{\mathbf{x+x^{\prime}}}\hat{S}^{z}_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}}-\braket{\hat{S}^{z}_{\mathbf{x+x^{\prime}}}}\braket{\hat{S}^{z}_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}}\Big], (6)

charge,

Cc​(𝐱)=1N​∑𝐱′[⟨n^𝐱+𝐱′z​n^𝐱′⟩−⟨n^𝐱+𝐱′⟩​⟨n^𝐱′z⟩],C_{c}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf x^{\prime}}\Big[\braket{\hat{n}^{z}_{\mathbf{x+x^{\prime}}}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}}-\braket{\hat{n}_{\mathbf{x+x^{\prime}}}}\braket{\hat{n}^{z}_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}}\Big], (7)

and pair correlations

for d-wave symmetrized pairs 22 2 An alternative definition of the pair correlation is given in references [34, 44], which defines a Cooper pair as (c^𝐱,↑​c^𝐱′,↓−c^𝐱,↓​c^𝐱′,↑)/2({\hat{c}}_{\bf x,\uparrow}{\hat{c}}_{\bf x^{\prime},\downarrow}-{\hat{c}}_{\bf x,\downarrow}{\hat{c}}_{\bf x^{\prime},\uparrow})/\sqrt{2}. Relative to our definition, this gives a factor of 2 enhancement of the pair correlation function.

Here ∑𝜹\sum_{\boldsymbol{\delta}} runs over nearest neighbors with sign⁡(𝜹)=+1\mathrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{\delta})=+1 for horizontal neighbors and −1-1 for vertical neighbors. We subtract D0​(𝐱,𝐱′)D_{0}({\bf x},{\bf x^{\prime}}), the normal state contribution from uncorrelated hopping: 33 3 The normal state contribution also contains a term that mixes spins ⟨c𝐱,↑†​c𝐱,↓⟩\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bf x,\uparrow}c_{\bf x,\downarrow}\rangle but this is zero for our simulations as they conserve SzS^{z}

For the phases in Fig. 1, the metal has no long range order, and the stripe phases have long-range charge and spin order. This manifests as a periodic modulation of the charge and spin correlation functions. When there is superconductivity, we expect an additional long range d-wave pairing order. This means that the spatial integral of the pair correlation function is proportional to the size of the system at large sizes and hence that the average pair correlation defined as:

C¯p≡1N​∑𝐱Cp​(𝐱){\bar{C}}_{p}\equiv\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf x}C_{p}({\bf x}) (10)

is non-zero in the thermodynamic limit:

limN→∞C¯p>0\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}{\bar{C}}_{p}>0 (11)

III Phase transition between filled stripes and partially-filled stripes with superconductivity

First we study the Hubbard model at U=8U=8 with hole-doping δ=1/8\delta=1/8, considering the phase diagram as a next neighbor hopping, t′<0t^{\prime}<0, is turned on. This is a relevant model for hole-doped cuprates such as La2-xSrxCuO4 or YBa2Cu3O7-x which typically have significant negative next-neighbor hopping, −0.4<t′<−0.1-0.4<t^{\prime}<-0.1 [32]. Building on prior work [18, 20, 45] , we consider two competing phases, a filled-stripe with a charge (spin) modulation of period λc⁡(s)=1​(2)/δ\lambda_{c(s)}=1(2)/\delta, and a half-filled stripe with a charge (spin) modulation of period λc⁡(s)=12×1​(2)/δ\lambda_{c(s)}=\frac{1}{2}\times 1(2)/\delta.

Since these phases break different symmetries, they are likely separated by a first order phase transition. Therefore, once we have a converged model in each phase, we use transfer learning to compare the energies as t′t^{\prime} is varied. Using a large 256256 site simulation cluster, we find a transition from a filled stripe to a half-filled stripe at t′=−0.1t^{\prime}=-0.1 (Fig.2c).

The details of the stripe order after training are shown in Fig.2a.-b. for t′=0t^{\prime}=0 and t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3 respectively. At t′=0t^{\prime}=0, we see that the spin correlations have period 1616 and the charge correlations have period 8, corresponding to a filled stripe. On the other hand, at t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3 the charge and spin periods are half as long, and therefore the domain walls are only half-filled with holes. While the amplitude of the spin modulation is roughly the same between the phases, the half-filled stripe has weaker charge modulation.

In figure 2d.-f. we show the d-wave pair correlations for both t′=0t^{\prime}=0 and t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3. We see in 2f. that the pair correlations for t′=−0.3t^{\prime}=-0.3 plateau to a value of 10−410^{-4}, in line with an order parameter of 𝒪⁡(10−2)\mathcal{O}(10^{-2}). This value is qualitatively consistent with the results of the recent CP-AFQMC+DMRG handshake collaboration [44], which also finds superconductivity coexisting with partially-filled stripes. We compare the pair correlations on a 128128 and a 256256 site cluster, finding that the asymptotic value is fairly consistent. This indicates that the 256256 site cluster is likely large enough to resolve off-diagonal long range order. In contrast, the pair correlations of the filled stripe phase decay to at least an order-of-magnitude smaller value and are nearly zero within our statistical error. Therefore, we expect that there is very little or no superconductivity in this phase (which is likely an insulator).

In order to show that the finding of superconductivity in the half-filled stripe is not biased by initialization, we document how the pair correlations in the half-filled stripe change with the strength of the d-wave pairing field Δ0\Delta_{0} used to initialize the orbitals.

For both optimizations with Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0, the optimization converges to a paired state, with fairly similar correlation functions. In contrast, for Δ0=0\Delta_{0}=0, the optimization finds a state with no pairing that has significantly higher energy.

IV Superconductivity in the overdoped Hubbard model

IV.1 Pair correlation function and finite size effects

As mentioned in the introduction, a much debated question is whether the pure Hubbard model has a superconducting ground state in any region of the parameter space. This is a relevant question for optical lattices which are beginning to reach effective temperatures where superconductivity might be detected[46].

At a formal level, the Hubbard model is known to be a d-wave superconductor for perturbatively small UU [27, 36]. However, the critical temperature is exponentially small in ∼(t/U)2\sim(t/U)^{2}, corresponding to very weak pairing.

An important practical goal is to figure out whether pairing becomes substantial once UU is increased beyond the perturbative limit, but not so large as to induce stripe ordering. This regime has been studied using diagrammatic Monte Carlo, which detects a BCS-like pairing instability for U/t<4U/t<4 [15].

We focus on the point U=4U=4, where the stripes are melted [45, 33], but UU is substantially beyond the weak coupling regime. We train HFPS wavefunctions starting from various mean field orbitals FF, corresponding to a filled stripe, a metal, and d-wave superconductors with various amounts of pairing. All of the initializations use the symmetry breaking cell of the filled stripe phase. The optimization finds two stable local minima; a superconducting phase with d-wave pairing and weak magnetic order, and a filled-stripe phase with no pairing. The superconductor is lower in energy by ∼0.5%\sim 0.5\%. The optimization energies on a 144144 site cluster starting from different initial conditions are shown below.

Even when the mean field orbitals are initialized in a metallic state by choosing Δ0=0,U0=1\Delta_{0}=0,U_{0}=1, the optimization finds a state with a significant amount of pairing. This contrasts with the half-filled stripe discussed in the previous section, where a pairing field was necessary to find the lowest-energy phase.

After verifying that the lowest energy state has superconducting order we examine how pair correlations change with system size. In Fig. 3b., the pair correlation functions (Eqn. 8) on 144144 and 288288 site clusters are compared. While the correlations on both clusters asymptote to non-zero values at fairly short distances, the 288288 site cluster decays to a much smaller value. The average pair correlation, C¯p{\bar{C}}_{p}, which should be non-zero for a superconductor in the thermodynamic limit, is displayed for as a horizontal line for reference. This decays by roughly a factor of 33 when the system size is doubled.

From this data, it is thus impossible to infer whether C¯p{\bar{C}}_{p} is finite in the limit of infinite system size. Therefore, a different way to measure pairing is necessary to resolve whether the ground state is a superconductor. We turn to weak coupling d-wave BCS theory [36, 27] for inspiration. The finite size effects from BCS theory have been studied extensively [1, 5, 43, 17]. In general they predict that pair correlations will decay with system size when the pair correlation length is much larger than the distance around the torus ℏ​vF/Δ≫N\hbar v_{F}/\Delta\gg\sqrt{N}. In this regime, pairs are fully delocalized on the torus such that they have a roughly equal probability of having each binding radius. As system size is increased, the pairs spread out, and the probability of a pair being local goes like 𝒪⁡(1/N)\mathcal{O}(1/N). The average pair correlation C¯p{\bar{C}}_{p}, which measures tunneling processes for local pairs, displays a 1/N21/N^{2} dependence on system size up to very large system sizes before eventually saturating – see appendix B for detailed analysis of d-wave BCS theory on finite size clusters.

In the following section, we show that at U=4,δ=1/6U=4,\delta=1/6 our simulations are still in the regime where the pair correlation length is larger than the distance around the torus. This explains the strong decay in the average pair correlation with system size. By moving to momentum space, we are able to construct a robust measure of pairing with weak finite size effects.

IV.2 Measuring momentum space pairing

Just as we defined a real space pair correlation function in Eqn. 8, we can also define a momentum space pair correlation,

M𝐤𝐤′=⟨p^𝐤†​p^𝐤′⟩−δ𝐤𝐤′​⟨n^𝐤↑⟩​⟨n^−𝐤↓⟩.M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=\langle{\hat{p}}^{\dagger}_{\bf k}{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}}\rangle-\delta_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}\langle{\hat{n}}_{\bf k\uparrow}\rangle\langle{\hat{n}}_{-\bf k\downarrow}\rangle.

Here p^𝐤=⟨c^𝐤,↑​c^−𝐤,↓⟩{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}=\langle{\hat{c}}_{\bf k,\uparrow}{\hat{c}}_{\bf-k,\downarrow}\rangle annihilates a momentum space pair and n^𝐤​σ=c^𝐤,σ†​c^𝐤,σ{\hat{n}}_{\bf k\sigma}={\hat{c}}^{\dagger}_{\bf k,\sigma}{\hat{c}}_{\bf k,\sigma} measures the occupation of a particle with momentum 𝐤{\bf k}. The normal state contribution is subtracted, such that M𝐤𝐤′=0M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=0 for free fermions. In contrast, for a uniform superconductor M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}} should be a rank-1 object that describes the independent creation and annihilation of pairs,

{limN→∞M𝐤𝐤′=p⁡(𝐤)​p​(𝐤′)SClimN→∞M𝐤𝐤′=0No SC\begin{cases}\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=p({\bf k})p({\bf k^{\prime}})&\textrm{SC}\\ \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=0&\textrm{No SC}\end{cases} (12)

Since MM involves two momentum space operators, it is a very expensive object for a real space code. Therefore, we only compute MM for a single simulation (U=4,δ=1/6U=4,\delta=1/6 on a 144144 cluster). In that case, we indeed find that MM is rank-1 to good approximation (see. App. A for details), which allows us to extract p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) using a Krylov method.

If we assume that M𝐤,𝐤′M_{\bf k,\bf k^{\prime}} has the rank-1 form in Eqn. 12, p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) can be computed in terms of a mixed real-momentum space correlation function

p⁡(𝐤)=cm​(𝐤)(1N​∑𝐤g𝐤​cm​(𝐤))1/2p({\bf k})=\frac{c_{m}({\bf k})}{(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k}g_{\bf k}c_{m}({\bf k}))^{1/2}} (13)
cm​(𝐤)=⟨d^†​p^𝐤⟩−1N​g𝐤​⟨n𝐤↑⟩​⟨n−𝐤,↓⟩c_{m}({\bf k})=\langle{\hat{d}}^{\dagger}{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle-\frac{1}{N}g_{\bf k}\langle n_{\bf k\uparrow}\rangle\langle n_{\bf-k,\downarrow}\rangle (14)

where g𝐤=(cos⁡(kx)−cos⁡(ky))/2g_{\bf k}=(\cos(k_{x})-\cos(k_{y}))/2 is the d-wave form factor. This estimator suppress the noise in p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) by a factor of N\sqrt{N} relative to using the dominant eigenvector of M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}.

We plot p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) at U=4U=4 on 144144 and 288288 site clusters in Fig. 3c.-d. For both system sizes, p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is sharply peaked at the Fermi surface and acquires a sign change under a 90​°90\degree rotation. In Fig. 3e.-f., we plot 1-dimensional cuts of p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) along relevant directions of the Fermi surface, and find that the value of p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is fairly similar across momenta common to both clusters. As seen in figure 3e. the 288 site cluster has additional k-points which help to resolve the peaks better.

Crucially, our data show that the momentum space pairing is roughly invariant with system size, in contrast to the large-distance behavior of the pair correlations. This therefore provides strong evidence for superconductivity. Since the peak in p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is under-resolved by the momentum space grid, the pair correlation length is longer than the maximum spacing on the torus. We can see this explicitly by writing the average pair correlation (equation 8) in terms of p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) as follows

C¯p=|1N​∑𝐤g𝐤​p​(𝐤)|2{\bar{C}}_{p}=\Bigg|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k}g_{\bf k}p({\bf k})\Bigg|^{2} (15)

Since p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is peaked at the anti-node of the Fermi surface, this sum is dominated by a single point leading to a large 1/N21/N^{2} contribution to the scaling with system size, hence explaining the distinct behavior of momentum-space and real-space measures of pairing.

IV.3 Fate of the uniform superconductor as U is increased

So far, our discussion has been limited to the point U=4U=4, where the pairs are still highly de-localized. For larger UU there is a competing filled-stripe phase, equivalent to the one in III, except with a different period λs⁡(c)=12​(6)\lambda_{s(c)}=12(6). A CP-AFQMC calculation, which considered the energetic competition between a non-superconducting metal and a stripe, estimates that there is a phase transition around U≈5U\approx 5 [45]. However, since the superconducting phase gains energy relative to the metal, this transition may be pushed up to larger UU.

We use transfer learning to train models at U=2,4,6,10,15U=2,4,6,10,15 on a 144144 site cluster. We consider the lowest energy stripe and superconducting phases specified in table 1 As UU is changed, the superconducting branch is always lowest in energy, but for U=10,15U=10,15 it also develops striped magnetic order. We probe this magnetic order by looking at the charge/spin structure factors,

Cc⁡(s)​(𝐤)=1N​∑𝐱ei​𝐤⋅𝐱​Cc⁡(s)​(𝐱).C_{c(s)}({\bf k})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf x}e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf x}}C_{c(s)}({\bf x}). (16)

For filled-stripe order, the structure factor peaks are at kc=(0,2​π/δ)k_{c}=(0,2\pi/\delta) and ks=(π−π/δ,π)k_{s}=(\pi-\pi/\delta,\pi). Fig. 4a.-b., shows the spin structure factor at U=6U=6, which has a dispersive peak at ksk_{s} and U=10U=10, which has a sharp peak at ksk_{s}. This may indicate a phase transition from a metal to a stripe phase. In Fig. 4c.-d., we plot one-dimensional cuts of the spin and charge structure factors that bisect these peaks. We see that going from U=6U=6 to U=10U=10, the spin structure factor peak at ksk_{s} becomes much sharper and the charge structure factor develops a kink at kck_{c} .

We plot relevant one-dimensional cuts of the momentum space pairing, p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) in Fig 4e.-f. As UU is increased the peaks tend to become less sharp, indicating a crossover away from the BCS regime. Again, there is a pronounced difference in the correlation function between U=6U=6 and U=10U=10. Once stripe order sets in, the pairs are de-localized in k-space, corresponding to a shorter correlation length.

In summary, at hole doping δ=1/6\delta=1/6 and t′=0t^{\prime}=0, we find evidence for a phase transition from a uniform superconductor to a phase with stripe order between U=6U=6 and U=10U=10. While this stripe phase still has significant pairing order on a 144144 site cluster, it remains to be seen whether this persists to the thermodynamic limit.

V Discussion

We have presented a study of superconductivity in the Hubbard model using a variational ansatz that combines Pfaffians with deep neural networks. Using fast Pfaffian algorithms [11, 42, 47], these simulations are scaled to large symmetric clusters of up to 288288 sites, allowing us to capture the ground state physics with minimal geometric bias. This has given new insight into the behavior of superconductors on finite sized tori.

We focus on two regimes of the Hubbard model, where the ground state may be a superconductor. First we look at the t−t′t-t^{\prime} model at strong coupling and low-doping with t′≤0t^{\prime}\leq 0, which is an effective model for hole doped cuprate superconductors. Here, we find that an insulating filled-stripe phase is stable at t′=0t^{\prime}=0, which transitions to a half-filled stripe with superconductivity around t′=−0.1t^{\prime}=-0.1. Using a Pfaffian based ansatz is crucial to represent this phase, as it has both magnetic and superconducting order.

Our results largely confirm the recent handshake study combining CP-AFQMC and DMRG [44], which found that partially-filled stripes coexist with superconductivity in the t′<0t^{\prime}<0 Hubbard model. Remarkably, this establishes consistency between three distinct computational methods on this challenging question. However, it should be noted that a recent study using DMRG on 6-leg cylinders reaches a different conclusion [22]. It is possible that this is due to the different geometry and boundary conditions used, which may favor charge- and spin-density ordering (see App. C.5 for a discussion of geometric effects in our simulations). This obviously deserves further comparative studies.

For the particular 16×1616\times 16 cluster we study, the half-filled stripe is favorable, but it is possible that different partially-filled stripe is favored in the thermodynamic limit. From a Hartree-Fock perspective, the filled stripe has a Mott gap while the partially-filled stripes have additional electrons in higher energy bands [41]. This may explain the difference in pairing between filled and partially-filled stripes. Future work should compare the energies and superconducting correlations among partially-filled stripes of different periods.

Next we discuss the pure Hubbard model with t′=0t^{\prime}=0, which is known to be a d-wave superconductor in the weak coupling limit for low doping levels[36, 3]. We look for superconductivity at intermediate couplings and higher doping[41], U=4U=4, δ=1/6\delta=1/6, where stripes are unlikely to be energetically competitive. We find that the ground state has short ranged magnetic order and pairing order on finite size clusters. While the correlations for spatially localized d-wave pairs decay like 1/N21/N^{2} with system size, the correlations between momentum space pairs are fairly size invariant. From this data, we conclude that the ground state at U=4U=4 is a superconductor with weakly bound pairs, such that the pair correlation length is longer than the circumference of the largest simulation cluster we can access. This data is in strong agreement with the diagrammatic Monte Carlo calculation in reference [15], which concludes the physics is governed by a BCS-like instability from a re-normalized Fermi-liquid state. We note that the magnitude of the local order parameter that can be inferred from Fig. 3b. is not inconsistent with those reported in reference [44] obtained by linear response to an applied pairing field (see Fig.13 in that reference).

Our data analysis introduces a novel approach for extracting information about superconductivity from finite size numerical simulations of the repulsive Hubbard model in regimes where the pairs are weakly bound. For the overdoped regime (δ=1/6\delta=1/6), we find that the pairing is better understood in momentum space than real space. Even as UU is increased far beyond the BCS regime, the momentum space pairing is still size invariant. This suggests that qualitative features of the weak coupling regime may apply beyond the range where it is controlled.

Our work establishes that Pfaffian-based NQS is an excellent tool for revealing superconducting order. Future NQS work should aim at further lowering the energies of these calculations by improving the optimization algorithms and documenting how the correlation functions change in this process.

Our ability to simulate large systems opens the possibility of using Pfaffian-based NQS for more realistic models of strongly correlated quantum materials. Applications such as three-band models for cuprates [16], as well as multi-orbital and moiré materials should be feasible.

Appendix A Efficiently measuring momentum space pairing

In the main text (equation IV.2) we define a momentum space pair correlation function M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}} which examines the correlations between creating and annihilating momentum space cooper pairs. While this correlation is prohibitively expensive for our largest system sizes, we examine its eigenvalue decomposition on a 144144 site cluster at U=4U=4,

M𝐤𝐤′=∑iλi​ei​(𝐤)​ei​(𝐤′).M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}e_{i}({\bf k})e_{i}({\bf k^{\prime}}). (17)

We plot the eigenvalues, λi\lambda_{i} in Fig. 5c. and see that there is a single dominant mode, as well as a distribution of subdominant eigenvalues. As we increase the number of samples used to compute M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}, the distribution of the subdominant eigenvalues narrows, indicating they are primarily due to noise. From this we include that, M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}} is already close to rank-1 on our 144 site system. Assuming that M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}} is a rank-1 object with statistical noise,

M𝐤𝐤′=p⁡(𝐤)​p​(𝐤′)+𝒩⁡(0,σ2),M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=p({\bf k})p({\bf k^{\prime}})+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), (18)

we consider the action of M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}} on the d-wave symmetric form factor,

1N​∑𝐤′M𝐤𝐤′​g𝐤′=p⁡(𝐤)​(𝐩⋅𝐠N)+𝒩⁡(0,σ2/N).\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k^{\prime}}M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k^{\prime}}=p({\bf k})\Big(\frac{{\bf p}\cdot{\bf g}}{N}\Big)+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}/N). (19)

Here, 𝐩⋅𝐠{\bf p}\cdot\bf{g} measures the overlap between p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) and the form factor g𝐤g_{\bf k}. Acting MM on the form factor extracts the shape of p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) and reduces the noise by N\sqrt{N}. In order to extract the norm, we multiply MM by the form factor on both sides,

1N2​∑𝐤,𝐤′g𝐤​M𝐤𝐤′​g𝐤′=(𝐩⋅𝐠N)2+𝒩⁡(0,σ2/N2)\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{\bf k,\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k}M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k^{\prime}}=\Big(\frac{{\bf p}\cdot{\bf g}}{N}\Big)^{2}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}/N^{2}) (20)

Using equation 14 we can express M​𝐠M{\bf g} and 𝐠​M​𝐠{\bf g}M{\bf g} in terms of a mixed estimator,

1N​∑𝐤′M𝐤𝐤′​g𝐤′=⟨d^†​p^𝐤⟩−1N​g𝐤​⟨n𝐤↑⟩​⟨n−𝐤,↓⟩=cm​(𝐤)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k^{\prime}}M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k^{\prime}}=\langle{\hat{d}}^{\dagger}{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle-\frac{1}{N}g_{\bf k}\langle n_{\bf k\uparrow}\rangle\langle n_{\bf-k,\downarrow}\rangle=c_{m}({\bf k}) (21)
1N2​∑𝐤′g𝐤​M𝐤𝐤′​g𝐤′=1N​∑𝐤g𝐤​cm​(𝐤)\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k}M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k}g_{\bf k}c_{m}({\bf k}) (22)

This brings us to equation 13, which estimates p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) in terms of a mixed real/momentum space correlation function. We can see that computing p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) from the mixed estimator has ∼σ/N\sim\sigma/\sqrt{N} noise whereas the largest eigenvalue of M𝐤𝐤′M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}} has ∼σ\sim\sigma noise. We compare the two measures of pairing in figure 5a.-b., and show they give similar results.

Appendix B Understanding pair correlations at small U from d-wave BCS theory

In this section we provide a brief introduction to d-wave BCS theory, which can describe the superconductor phenomenologically for small UU. The dominant finite size effects can be understood by considering the mean field theory with a finite number of k-points.

B.1 A brief pedagogical description of BCS theory

The d-wave BCS Hamiltonian, which perturbs free fermions with a small attractive interaction of d-wave symmetry, is written as follows,

ℋ=∑σ∑𝐤(ϵk−μ)​n^𝐤+∑𝐤𝐤′V𝐤,𝐤′​p^𝐤†​p^𝐤′\mathcal{H}=\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{\bf k}(\epsilon_{k}-\mu){\hat{n}}_{\bf k}+\sum_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}V_{{\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}}}{\hat{p}}^{\dagger}_{\bf k}{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}} (23)

where,

V𝐤,𝐤′=−VN​g𝐤​g𝐤′V_{{\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}}}=-\frac{V}{N}g_{\bf k}g_{\bf k^{\prime}} (24)

We apply a mean field decoupling to solve this Hamiltonian

ℋB​C​S=∑𝐤[∑σ(ϵk−μ)​n^𝐤,σ−(Δ𝐤​p^𝐤†+H.C.)]\mathcal{H}_{BCS}=\sum_{\bf k}\Bigg[\sum_{\sigma}(\epsilon_{k}-\mu){\hat{n}}_{\bf k,\sigma}-\big(\Delta_{\bf k}{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}^{\dagger}+\textrm{H.C.}\big)\Bigg] (25)

where

Δ𝐤=−∑𝐤′V𝐤𝐤′⟨p^𝐤′⟩.\Delta_{\bf k}=-\sum_{\bf k^{\prime}}V_{{\bf kk^{\prime}}}\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}}\rangle. (26)

While the true BCS Hamiltonian in equation 23 conserves particle number, the mean field treatment breaks this symmetry and allows for an anomalous expectation value of ⟨p𝐤⟩\langle p_{\bf k}\rangle.

Using the separable form in equation 24, we see that the self-consistent field is proportional to the form factor, Δ𝐤=Δ​g𝐤\Delta_{\bf k}=\Delta g_{\bf k} where

Δ=VN​∑𝐤′g𝐤′​⟨p^𝐤′⟩\Delta=\frac{V}{N}\sum_{\bf k^{\prime}}g_{\bf k^{\prime}}\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}}\rangle (27)

Solving the bilinear Hamiltonian in equation 25 gives the solution

⟨p^𝐤⟩=Δ𝐤2​((ϵ𝐤−μ)2+Δ𝐤2)1/2\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle=\frac{\Delta_{\bf k}}{2((\epsilon_{\bf k}-\mu)^{2}+\Delta_{\bf k}^{2})^{1/2}} (28)

Combining these equations leads to the gap equation which relates Δ\Delta to V,

1=VN​∑𝐤g𝐤22​((ϵ𝐤−μ)2+Δ2​g𝐤2)1/21=\frac{V}{N}\sum_{\bf k}\frac{g_{\bf k}^{2}}{2((\epsilon_{\bf k}-\mu)^{2}+\Delta^{2}g_{\bf k}^{2})^{1/2}} (29)

The chemical potential is set by the number equation,

n=12​N​∑𝐤(1−ϵ𝐤−μOPEN((ϵ𝐤−μ)2+Δ2​g𝐤)2)1/2)n=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\bf k}\Bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon_{\bf k}-\mu}{((\epsilon_{\bf k}-\mu)^{2}+\Delta^{2}g_{\bf k})^{2})^{1/2}}\Bigg) (30)

We can also compute the traditional d-wave order parameter from BCS theory

⟨d⟩=1N​∑𝐤g𝐤​⟨p^𝐤⟩\langle d\rangle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k}g_{\bf k}\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle (31)

B.2 Fitting pair correlations to BCS theory

In this section, we fit our momentum space pairing estimator p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) at U=2U=2 to the predictions of mean field BCS theory. In BCS theory, the momentum space pair creation and annihilation processes are fully decoupled. For example,

⟨p^𝐤†​p^𝐤′⟩=⟨p^𝐤⟩​⟨p^𝐤′⟩+δ𝐤,𝐤′​⟨n^𝐤,↑⟩​⟨n^−𝐤,↓⟩\langle{\hat{p}}^{\dagger}_{\bf k}{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}}\rangle=\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}}\rangle+\delta_{\bf k,\bf k^{\prime}}\langle{\hat{n}}_{\bf k,\uparrow}\rangle\langle{\hat{n}}_{\bf-k,\downarrow}\rangle (32)

which gives

M𝐤𝐤′=⟨p^𝐤⟩​⟨p^𝐤′⟩M_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}=\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k^{\prime}}\rangle (33)

Therefore, we expect M𝐤,𝐤′M_{\bf k,\bf k^{\prime}} to become low rank as we approach the BCS theory limit. Furthermore, we can compute the mixed estimator

p⁡(𝐤)=⟨p^𝐤⟩p({\bf k})=\langle\hat{p}_{\bf k}\rangle (34)

and finally the pair-pair correlation function

C¯p=1N2​(∑𝐤𝐤′⟨p^𝐤⟩​g𝐤)2{\bar{C}}_{p}=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\Big(\sum_{\bf k\bf k^{\prime}}\langle{\hat{p}}_{\bf k}\rangle g_{\bf k}\Big)^{2} (35)

The finite size effects of C¯p{\bar{C}}_{p} can be divided into two categories,

  • •

    The amplitude and shape of p⁡(𝐤)p(\bf k). The peak location is specified by the chemical potential μ\mu, which is set by the equation 30. The scale is set by Δ\Delta

  • •

    The sum in equation 35 strongly depends on the location of allowed k-points in the Brillouin zone.

In the main text, we compare two system sizes, where the chemical potentials are exactly the same for Δ=0\Delta=0,

μ144,288​(Δ=0)=−2​(1+cos⁡(5​π/6))=−0.2679\mu_{144,288}(\Delta=0)=-2(1+\cos(5\pi/6))=-0.2679 (36)

As long as Δ\Delta is small relative to tt (we find Δ/t∼0.01\Delta/t\sim 0.01) , this chemical potential does not change very much from the Δ=0\Delta=0 value. Therefore, the two geometries we consider provide an apples-to-apples comparison for p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}). Since p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is size invariant, the effective Δ\Delta is size invariant.

We demonstrate this point more explicitly by fitting to BCS theory at U=2U=2,

Δ,μ=argminΔ,μ[∑𝐤(p⁡(𝐤)−p𝐤B​C​S​(μ,Δ))2σp⁡(𝐤)2+λ(n−nB​C​S(μ,δ))2]\begin{split}\Delta,\mu=\textrm{argmin}_{\Delta,\mu}\Bigg[\sum_{\bf k}\frac{\Big(p({\bf k})-p_{\bf k}^{BCS}(\mu,\Delta)\Big)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}_{p({\bf k})}}+\\ \lambda\Big(n-n^{BCS}(\mu,\delta)\Big)^{2}\Bigg]\end{split}

Here we do an SNR-weighted fit, where p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is the sampled average from our neural network wavefunction and σp⁡(𝐤)2\sigma^{2}_{p({\bf k})}describes our measurement error for p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}). This is important because p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) tends to be noisier outside of the Fermi surface. The second term is added to enforce the constraint that the chemical potential μ\mu agrees with the particle number. We take λ\lambda to be extremely large.

Fig. 6a-b. shows the pairing order parameter, Δ\Delta, computed from a fit to BCS theory and C¯p​(|𝐱|>3){\bar{C}}_{p}(|{\bf x}|>3) for both system sizes at U=2U=2. We see that while Δ\Delta is roughly system size invariant, C¯p​(|𝐱|>3){\bar{C}}_{p}(|{\bf x}|>3) decays strongly with system size. In Fig. 6c-d. we show side-by-side color plots of p(k) computed with NQS, and BCS-theory respectively. We can see that the BCS-theory fit with Δ≈0.01\Delta\approx 0.01 models the data very well. We find that at U=4U=4 and U=6U=6 this fit unsurprisingly degrades in quality.

B.3 How does finite size BCS change with Δ\Delta

Now that we’ve established that pairing is fairly size invariant based on our numerical data, we document the difficulty of extrapolating a local pairing order parameter.

We solve the mean field BCS equations for fixed Δ\Delta and show how C¯p{\bar{C}}_{p} scales with system size. First, equation 30 is solved to set the chemical potential, then long range pair correlations are computed from equation 35 . The results are shown in figure 7

In general, the pair correlations decay with system size, but there are also oscillations. The pair correlations are larger on small systems because the momentum space grid is too coarse to resolve the sharp peak in ⟨p𝐤⟩\langle p_{\bf k}\rangle. Therefore, points that are near the Fermi surface are overweighted in the sum in equation 35. The occasional upward oscillations occur when a new k-points are introduced that are close to the Fermi-surface. From this data, we see that a system size extrapolation of the traditional d-wave order parameter from C¯p{\bar{C}}_{p} is a fool’s errand, as there is strong finite size effects up to ∼1000\sim 1000 sites.

Appendix C Supplementary data

This section contains additional data that has shaped our understanding of superconductivity in the Hubbard model.

C.1 A real space perspective on the BCS-like superconductor

In the main text we showed that the momentum space pairing, p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is fairly size invariant, while the pair correlations for local d-wave pairs Cp​(𝐱)C_{p}({\bf x}) decay with system size. We can understand this effect from a real space perspective by introducing a real space pairing amplitude p⁡(𝐱)p({\bf x}), which acts as a proxy for the probability of annihilating a pairs with displacement 𝐱{\bf x}. We compute p⁡(𝐱)p({\bf x}) by Fourier transforming p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k})

p⁡(𝐱)=1N​∑𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐱​p​(𝐤)p({\bf x})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf k}e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf x}}p({\bf k}) (37)

We plot p⁡(𝐱)p({\bf x}) on 144144 and 288288 site clusters at U=4U=4 in Fig. 8. On the 288 site cluster the nearest neighbors are rotated by 45​°45\degree relative to the 144 site cluster. Here, we see that the pairs are almost completely de-localized. When the system size is doubled, the pairs delocalize further and the effective amplitude of annihilating a particular pair is halved. This leads to a 1/N21/N^{2} scaling in pair correlations, which create and annihilate a next-neighbor pair.

C.2 Size invariance across different U

For all values of UU that we study, the momentum space pairing, p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is roughly system size invariant. In figure 9, p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) is shown on 144144 and 288288 site clusters for different values of UU. By U=6U=6 the peak in p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) has become much broader, such that the shape can no longer be explained by BCS theory, but the size invariance remains.

C.3 Momentum space pairing and finite size effects for the half-filled stripe superconductor

We show a similar momentum space pairing analysis for the half-filled stripe phase to indicate why the pairing order parameter has likely converged. As shown in 2f. the asymptotic value of the pair correlation functions is roughly invariant going from a 128 to a 256 site cluster.

We can also look at p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) (Eqn. 13), and see that it is also fairly system size invariant between the 128128 and 256256 site clusters. In Fig. 10 we plot the effective order parameter, C¯p\sqrt{\bar{C}_{p}} as a function of three system sizes, as well as p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) on 128128 and 256256 site clusters. We see that p⁡(𝐤)p({\bf k}) has no strong peaks, which indicates that the integral is unlikely to change much as more k-points are introduced.

C.4 Partially filed stripe normal state

By starting our optimization from an unpaired trial wavefunction, we can also find a “normal state” for the partially-filled stripe phase. This phase has ∼1%\sim 1\% higher energy than the superconducting phase, and very similar charge/spin correlation functions. In figure 11a., we plot the pair correlations for both phases, showing that the normal state has no superconductivity. In figure 11b.-c., we plot relevant 1-D cuts of the charge and spin structure factors. We see that the normal state has slightly enhanced charge/spin structure factor peaks.

C.5 Effects of changing lattice geometry

In order to understand the effect of lattice geometry, we also trained models for the superconducting and stripe phases on a 24×424\times 4 torus. We find that the energies are extremely comparable, with the stripe phase slightly favored,

This is a notably different result from the 12×1212\times 12 torus (table 7) where the superconductor is ∼0.5%\sim 0.5\% lower in energy. Therefore, we see that boundary effects can profoundly affect the location of the stripe transition. While this transition is between U=6U=6 and U=10U=10 on the 12×1212\times 12 cluster (see Sec. IV.3), it is below U=4U=4 on the 24×424\times 4 torus.

In figure 13 we show pair correlations for the superconducting phase on this geometry. We see that the pair correlation function oscillates, precluding an obvious way to estimate long range order. These differences have motivated us to focus our simulations on symmetric tori.

Appendix D Optimization details

D.1 Training procedure

We optimize our HFPS wavefunction in a two step procedure as done in reference [11]. First we optimize the mean field using exact gradient techniques. Using the mean field orbitals FF, the two-body expectation values ⟨c𝐱,σ†​c𝐱′,σ′⟩\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bf x,\sigma}c_{\bf x^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle, ⟨c𝐱,σ​c𝐱′,σ′⟩\langle c_{\bf x,\sigma}c_{\bf x^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle can be computed. Expectation values of four body operators can then be computed with Wick’s theorem. This allows us to compute an energy function E⁡(F,H)E(F,H), where HH is defined in Eqn. 5, and use automatic differentiation to update F in order to move downhill in the energy landscape,

Δ​F=−dd​F​(E​(F,H))\Delta F=-\frac{d}{dF}(E(F,H)) (38)

We typically minimize this function for 50K steps until the energy is fairly converged.

Typically this optimization is much more efficient when FF is in a block circulant form corresponding to a particular mean field order. For the t-t’ model at δ=1/8\delta=1/8, we try both fully-filled and half-filled stripes. For higher dopings, we always use a unit cell that accommodates a fully filled stripe.

It is important to add a d-wave pinning field to HH in order to represent a superconducting phase. This is because the pairing only enters E⁡(F,H)E(F,H) through a quadratic form.

U0​⟨c𝐱↑†​c𝐱↑​c𝐱↓†​c𝐱↓⟩=U0​⟨c𝐱↑†​c𝐱↓†⟩​⟨c𝐱↓​c𝐱↑⟩+…=U0​⟨c𝐱↓​c𝐱↑⟩2+…\begin{split}U_{0}\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\uparrow}c_{\bf x\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\downarrow}c_{\bf x\downarrow}\rangle=\\ U_{0}\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{\bf x\downarrow}\rangle\langle c_{\bf x\downarrow}c_{\bf x\uparrow}\rangle+...=U_{0}\langle c_{\bf x\downarrow}c_{\bf x\uparrow}\rangle^{2}+...\end{split}

For U0>0U_{0}>0 this is always minimized when ⟨c𝐱↓​c𝐱↑⟩=0\langle c_{\bf x\downarrow}c_{\bf x\uparrow}\rangle=0.

D.2 Hyperparameters

All neural network were trained via imaginary time evolution starting from the mean field states specified in the main text. We implement this using the MinSR algorithm [8, 37], with rt​o​l=10−12r_{tol}=10^{-12}. The learning rate for all calculations was η=0.005\eta=0.005. For each calculation we used 88 hidden fermions, 1818 features and 88 residual layers of HFPS + GCNN architecture described in reference [11].
